title: Bayes Theorem and Conditional Probability
breadcrumb: Probability → Bayes theorem and conditional probability
engineName: Probability — conditioning, partitions and posterior updating
objectives: Compute conditional probabilities using the multiplication rule.
Use partitions and the law of total probability.
Apply Bayes theorem to reverse conditional probabilities.
Interpret prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV.
Recognise independence and avoid base-rate neglect in diagnostic problems.
traps: P(A|B) and P(B|A) are not interchangeable.
The total-probability denominator must include every partition cell.
PPV depends on prevalence; sensitivity alone does not determine it.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are not independent.

tricks: Draw a 2×2 table for diagnostic tests.
Convert specificity to false-positive rate before calculation.
Write the partition before using total probability.
shortcuts: Out of 10,000, translate prevalence into counts.
Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.
Check that posterior probabilities sum to one across the partition.
remember: Rare conditions can have low PPV despite high sensitivity.

howto: Define the target cause and evidence event, write the prior and likelihoods, build the total-probability denominator and only then apply Bayes. For diagnostic tests use a 2×2 table or out-of-10,000 counts to keep prevalence visible.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four foundations
scenes.objective: Retrieve events, intersections and conditional probability.
body: Conditional probability changes the sample space to the event already known to have occurred.
Bayes theorem reverses the direction of conditioning; total probability supplies its denominator.

ask.q: What event appears in the denominator of P(A|B)?
ask.nudge: It is the event you already know has occurred.

refresh: Positive-probability mutually exclusive events are dependent.

items.recall: A disjoint, exhaustive collection of events.
refresh: Every outcome belongs to exactly one cell.

scenes.title: A positive test is not a diagnosis
body: A test's sensitivity is the chance of a positive result among diseased people. It is not the chance of disease among positive people.
The posterior denominator includes true positives and false positives. When prevalence is low, healthy people may greatly outnumber diseased people.
Bayes theorem combines prior prevalence and likelihoods; ignoring the prior is the base-rate fallacy.

scenario.teaser: A screening test is accurate, but the posterior probability remains low.
scenario.title: The base rate is part of the evidence
body: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects 95% of true cases and correctly clears 90% of healthy people. One patient tests positive.
Out of 10,000 people, about 100 have the disease and 95 test positive. Of 9,900 healthy people, 990 test positive because the false-positive rate is 10%.
There are 1,085 positive results, of which only 95 are true cases. The posterior is 95/1,085≈8.76%, not 95%.
Sensitivity is P(+|D), not P(D|+). Bayes reverses the conditioning and includes all sources of positive evidence.
scenario.q: Why is P(D|+) much lower than 95% sensitivity?
scenario.answer: Because the many healthy people who test positive contribute to the denominator; the prior prevalence is only 1%.

ask.q: Why does prevalence matter to PPV?
ask.nudge: Count how many healthy people can test positive.

blocks.body: If A₁,…,A_k are disjoint and exhaustive, P(B)=ΣP(B|A_i)P(A_i). The partition must cover the sample space.
P(A_j|B)=P(B|A_j)P(A_j)/P(B). Posterior = likelihood × prior / total evidence.
Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. For a positive test, LR+=sensitivity/(1−specificity).
A,B independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0. Mutually exclusive positive-probability events are not independent.
Sensitivity=P(+|D); specificity=P(−|Dᶜ); false-positive rate=1−specificity; PPV=P(D|+), which depends on prevalence.

flow.title: Bayes calculation

nodes.label: Define cause A and evidence B

flow.note: The denominator sums evidence over every cell in the partition.

ask.q: Why does Bayes require a denominator?
ask.nudge: The likelihood contributions must be normalised across all possible causes.

scenes.title: Worked example — rare disease screening
scenes.problem: A disease prevalence is 1%; sensitivity is 95% and specificity is 90%. Find P(D|+).

steps.why: Include true positives and false positives.
A positive result raises the prior from 1% to 8.76%, but most positives are false.

scenes.after: Sensitivity is P(+|D); the requested posterior is P(D|+).

ask.q: What is the false-positive rate when specificity is 90%?

scenes.title: Complete the Bayes denominator
scenes.objective: Construct the posterior step by step.
scenes.problem: For a test with prevalence 1%, sensitivity 95% and specificity 90%, complete the PPV calculation.

steps.why: The denominator includes true and false positives.

scenes.after: The denominator is the total evidence probability, not just the true-positive term.

blocks.body: Posterior odds = prior odds × LR, where LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity) for a positive test.
A and B are independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.
If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, P(A∩B)=0 while P(A)P(B)>0; therefore they are not independent.

ask.q: Can two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities be independent?
ask.nudge: Compare zero intersection with the product of their positive probabilities.

scenes.title: On your own — machine origin
scenes.problem: Machine M₁ produces 60% of items with 2% defect rate; M₂ produces 40% with 5% defect rate. Given a defective item, find P(M₂|D).
hints: Divide the numerator by total defect probability.
scenes.check: The posterior is 62.5%, not 5% or 40%; it combines likelihood and prior and normalises.

scenario.teaser: A defective item is traced back to one of two machines.
scenario.title: Reverse the conditioning direction
body: Machine M₁ produces 60% of items with a 2% defect rate. M₂ produces 40% with a 5% defect rate. An item is found defective.
The known quantities are P(D|M₁), P(D|M₂), P(M₁) and P(M₂); the requested probability is P(M₂|D).
Total defect probability is .02×.60+.05×.40=.032. The M₂ defective contribution is .05×.40=.02.
Thus P(M₂|D)=.02/.032=.625. Define the partition, compute the denominator and only then reverse the conditioning.

solution.why: This is the M₂ defective contribution.

items.why: False: sensitivity is P(+|D); PPV is P(D|+).
True: it is the true-negative probability.

items.claim: PPV depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and specificity.
items.why: True: Bayes denominator contains the prior prevalence.

items.claim: Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are independent.
items.why: False: intersection is zero but the product of probabilities is positive.

items.claim: Bayes denominator sums likelihood-weighted priors over a partition.

scenes.title: Transfer problem — PPV and NPV
scenes.problem: A test has prevalence 2%, sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. Find PPV=P(D|+) and NPV=P(Dᶜ|−).
scenes.check: False-positive rate is 5%. NPV is about 99.79%, PPV about 26.87%.
